summary: Discovery focused on cost/unit economics for Redwood hosted vs Dedicated/Private. Customer wants to understand per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and budget constraints tied to expected 10k req/day load. Security and data residency are gating for Private; finance wants ROI comparisons and committed cost for Dedicated.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 14:30 UTC, Duration ~42 minutes. Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Evelyn (Pinnacle Head of ML), Marco (Infra Lead), Nora (Head of Finance)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, with liam our se, how's it going?
[00:05] Evelyn: good thanks, excited to dig into costing — we run a lot of inference for trading signals, so cost per unit matters.
[00:12] Liam: awesome, quick agenda — run through current stack, traffic profile, goals, then walk through hosted vs dedicated vs private economics and batching/caching levers, end with next steps.
[00:20] Marco: quick note, we care about latency under 200 ms p95 for short prompts, but most of our runs are batched overnight for re-scoring. We also have a smaller real-time path.
[00:30] Nora: and i'm mainly here for budget/commit questions — want to understand fixed vs variable spend.

[00:45] Maya: great. can you give a thumbnail of traffic/reqs?
[00:50] Marco: sure — avg 10k inference calls/day, 70% re-runs (longer contexts) overnight; typical prompt 300 tokens in, 150 tokens out. realtime path is about 1k calls/day with strict latency.
[01:10] Evelyn: also, model types — we're evaluating both open models and some LLMs from hosted vendors. quantization is something we can do on our side but would like advice.

[01:30] Liam: ok so cost levers: per-token pricing (hosted), batching & continuous batching (dedicated + hosted), KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts, and quantization/plex of model variants. Hosted gives simple per-token, Dedicated gives lower unit cost at commit but requires reserved capacity.
[01:50] Marco: can you share rough per-token numbers for hosted and dedicated? just ballpark.
[01:55] Maya: ballpark examples we typically share — for a medium open-generation model: hosted might be ~ $0.0015 per output token and $0.0005 per input token; Dedicated effective per-token can be 40-60% lower depending on utilization and batch sizes. these are examples, we'll send exact sheet.
[02:20] Nora: 40-60% lower is attractive but what's the break-even in terms of commit?
[02:24] Liam: depends on utilization. e.g., at 60% utilization of a dedicated pool amortized over commit, you might break even around 50k-100k tokens/day depending on model and tok lengths. also batch sizes matter a lot for throughput.

[02:45] Evelyn: walk me through how batching reduces cost — is it just GPU throughput improvements?
[02:50] Liam: yes — continuous batching increases tokens/sec and amortizes kernel launch and memory overhead; for autoregressive models you get big win with output length and batch size. we also do KV caching for prefixes — if you have repeated context (like orderbook snapshots) you can cache the KV states so repeated tokens are cheaper.
[03:15] Marco: we do a lot of prefix reuse, do you call that KV cache? sometimes i see 'KV cash' in notes haha.
[03:20] Liam: yep, KV cache — apologies, the transcriber sometimes writes cash. it stores key/value tensors so you don't recompute for prefix tokens. in practice if 60% of tokens are repeated, you cut compute a lot.

[03:40] Nora: from finance side, we need three comparisons: hosted pay-as-you-go; dedicated reserved monthly commit (with discounts); private (on-prem/vpc) total cost incl infra + ops.
[03:55] Maya: agreed. Private often shifts costs to infra capex/ops — benefits are control, data residency, and sometimes lower long-term unit costs but higher upfront. we'll include a TCO sheet.

[04:10] Evelyn: any constraints on function-calling or streaming that changes cost?
[04:14] Liam: function calling doesn't materially change per-token math but streaming can increase bids for long-lived connections; main levers remain batch size and model choice. also we have quantized variants for dedicated/private that run at lower memory and cost.

[04:35] Marco: question about SLA & fallback — if a dedicated pool is full what happens for real-time path?
[04:40] Maya: you can configure smart routing — realtime can be routed to higher-priority capacity or hosted as overflow; you can set automatic fallback to hosted model variants. that impacts unit cost for overflow but preserves latency SLOs.

[05:00] Nora: what about security — SOC2, SSO, KMS? important for our compliance.
[05:05] Maya: Hosted is SOC2 and we support SSO/SAML and customer-managed KMS for key control. Dedicated gives stronger isolation; Private gives full customer control, audit logs, and HSM/KMS integrations. we'll share our security pack.

[05:25] Evelyn: ok can we run a small benchmark to quantify per-token cost for our mix?
[05:30] Liam: yes — typical plan: we run their 10k/day profile over 48 hours, measure p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, batching efficiency, and effective unit cost. we'll need request distribution and sample prompts.
[05:45] Marco: we'll share logs and a sample of prompts, but need NDA?
[05:48] Maya: we already have an MSA in motion, but i'll confirm with legal; we can do anonymized runs too.

[06:00] Nora: and for dedicated commits, what's typical contract length and penalties?
[06:05] Maya: usually monthly or annual reserves; discounts increase with longer terms; penalties vary but we can model a flexible burst/buffer. we'll send a sample term sheet.

[06:20] Evelyn: can you explain caching vs batching again with a concrete example? say 300 in /150 out, prefix reused 50% of tokens.
[06:30] Liam: sure — without caching each request computes 450 tokens. with 50% prefix reuse, maybe only 225 tokens compute. if batching groups 8 requests, kernel throughput improves so cost/token drops again. combined you can see 3-5x reduction in compute cost vs naive single-call serving.

[06:55] Marco: how do token counting differences between providers affect cost? we sometimes get surprised by tokenization differences.
[07:00] Maya: good point — tokenization can vary; we recommend measuring with a consistent tokenizer. we'll provide tooling and sample tokenization scripts.

[07:15] Nora: what about embeddings vs generation costs? we use embeddings for similarity searches, a lot of smaller tokens but large volume.
[07:22] Liam: embeddings are billed differently usually per embedding unit; they're cheaper per unit but volumes add up. for high-volume embeddings, Dedicated or on-prem quantized encoder models can be much cheaper.

[07:40] Evelyn: are there specific model variants you'd recommend for our workload?
[07:45] Liam: for low-latency re-scoring, a quantized 8-bit generation model on Dedicated is good; for overnight batch runs, larger unquantized variant may be fine. we'll include model recommendations.

[08:00] Marco: curious about autoscaling on Dedicated, do you allow burst to hosted?
[08:05] Maya: yes — you can configure burst capacity to hosted to handle spikes; you pay hosted rates for overflow. that gives a safety valve without overcommitting.

[08:20] Evelyn: any gotchas around prefix caching and multi-tenant privacy?
[08:25] Liam: cache is per-customer per-model or isolated by tenant, so no cross-tenant leakage. Private gives you even more control.

[08:35] Nora: ok, finance wants example ROI: if we move 60% of tokens to dedicated, what's the expected monthly savings?
[08:40] Liam: rough calc: if hosted blended is $0.0012/token and Dedicated effective $0.0006, 60% shift at your volume could save ~30-40% of compute spend; exacts depend on token lengths and idle overhead. we'll run numbers with your data.

[09:02] Maya: recap — collect traffic profile, sample prompts, current infra costs, and we'll run a benchmark + TCO sheet. We'll send pricing and security docs.

[09:12] Marco: i'll share infra cost & sample prompts by Monday.

[09:15] Nora: finance will want the spend model and amortized break-even.

[09:18] Maya: noted — we'll include break-even spreadsheet with sensitivities.

[09:25] Evelyn: timeline — can we aim for benchmark next week and results the following week?

[09:28] Liam: yes depending on data handoff.

[09:35] Maya: any final concerns?

[09:37] Nora: just ensure security docs hit our compliance mailbox.
[09:40] Maya: will do. thanks all.

[09:45] (meeting ends)

Notes & artifacts referenced: redwood-pricing-sheet (link sent after), security-pack.pdf (link), benchmark-plan.xlsx (to be created).

Transcript imperfections: occasional misattribution of speaker names and tokenization of 'KV cache' as 'KV cash'. Some filler words and overlaps.

End of transcript.
